Picture Worlds: Storytelling on Greek, Moche,
and Maya Pottery is the first book to examine
the terracotta vessels of the ancient Greeks,
Moche, and Maya side by side. Though
separate in both space and time, each of these
societies utilized the curving surfaces of
painted ceramics to visualize their myths and
beliefs. The volume provides an overview of
each culture, analyzes pottery production and
use, and takes a close look at the iconography.
It provides readers with the resources neces-
sary to explore the “picture worlds” of Greek,
Moche, and Maya pottery, and offers fresh
insights into the dynamic potential of narra-
tive images.

surprising similarities may arise, and the questions we ask of
one culture may prompt different responses for the other two.
Why decorate utilitarian shapes with complex scenes of mortal
or mythical activity? What social practices did these painted
vessels—made for feasting, for drinking, for ritual or funerary
purposes—make possible? What narratives, beliefs, or ideas did
the scenes convey? How might they relate to written or verbal
forms of communication? How did painters convey place, or the
passage of time, on the curving surface of a pot? And how did
users engage with these painted scenes?
    These are just a few of the lines of inquiry that arise
through the juxtaposition of Greek, Moche, and Maya painted
pottery. This volume and its accompanying exhibition—gen­
erously supported by Jeffrey P. Cunard and the Getty Patron
Program, and by Charles and Ellen Steinmetz in honor of
Professor Christopher B. Donnan—encourage the exchange of
methodological approaches across the traditional structures
of university departments or curatorial specialisms. The three
cultures differ substantially—not only in terms of their political
and social organization, and the existence, if any, of textual
sources, but also through modern histories of study, collecting,
and display. Faced with such diversity, definitive answers may
prove elusive, but—as is manifest in the collaborative approach

Picture Worlds is the first book to examine
the elaborately decorated terracotta vessels
of the ancient Greek, Moche, and Maya
civilizations. Although these societies were
separated by space and time, they all employed
pottery as a means for telling stories and
giving visual form to core myths and beliefs.
But why did these communities reach for
painted ceramics as a medium for communi-
cation? How were the vessels produced
and used? How can we understand these
“picture worlds” today? In this book, experts
explore these foundational questions, offer-
ing introductions to the three civilizations
and examining the painted imagery. Readers
will be rewarded with a richer understand-
ing of each of these societies, fascinating
insights into their cultural commonalities
and differences, and fresh perspectives on
image making and storytelling—practices
that remain vibrant to this day.
